title: What is a trigger (BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF), its use cases, advantages, and disadvantages?
shortTitle: Triggers (BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF) — Use Cases, Advantages, Disadvantages

s1_definition.profdef: A trigger is procedural code stored in the database that automatically executes in response to a data event — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on a table (and in some engines DDL or login events). It fires `BEFORE` the event (to validate or modify the incoming row), `AFTER` the event (to react, such as auditing), or `INSTEAD OF` the event (to redirect it, typically on a view). Triggers enforce rules, maintain audit trails, and keep derived data consistent without the application having to remember to do so.
s1_definition.analogy: A trigger is like a silent back-office rule at National Bank of India that fires by itself whenever something happens to a record. BEFORE a deposit is written, a rule can clean or reject it (validate the amount is positive). AFTER a deposit is written, a rule can automatically log it to the audit book. INSTEAD OF someone trying to change a read-only summary report (a view), a rule redirects the change to the real underlying tables. Nobody calls these rules; they run automatically on the event.
s1_definition.oneliner: A trigger is database code that fires automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE — BEFORE to validate/modify, AFTER to react/audit, INSTEAD OF to redirect (usually on views).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A trigger is procedural code stored in the database that automatically executes in response to a data event — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on a table (and in some engines DDL or login events). It fires `BEFORE` the event (to validate or modify the incoming row), `AFTER` the event (to react, such as auditing), or `INSTEAD OF` the event (to redirect it, typically on a view). Triggers enforce rules, maintain audit trails, and keep derived data consistent without the application having to remember to do so.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A trigger is like a silent back-office rule at National Bank of India that fires by itself whenever something happens to a record. BEFORE a deposit is written, a rule can clean or reject it (validate the amount is positive). AFTER a deposit is written, a rule can automatically log it to the audit book. INSTEAD OF someone trying to change a read-only summary report (a view), a rule redirects the change to the real underlying tables. Nobody calls these rules; they run automatically on the event.

**One line to remember:** A trigger is database code that fires automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE — BEFORE to validate/modify, AFTER to react/audit, INSTEAD OF to redirect (usually on views).

sections.s2_technical:
A trigger is bound to a table (or view) and an event and runs automatically when that event occurs. The timing determines what it can do. A BEFORE trigger runs before the row change is written, so it can validate the data and reject the operation by raising an error, or modify the incoming values (for example, normalize or default a column); it sees the proposed new values and can change them. An AFTER trigger runs once the change is already applied, so it cannot alter the row but can react to it — writing an audit record, updating a summary table, or sending a notification. An INSTEAD OF trigger replaces the triggering action entirely and is used mainly on views that are otherwise not updatable, translating an insert or update on the view into the appropriate changes on the underlying base tables. Triggers can be row-level (fire once per affected row, with access to OLD and NEW row images) or statement-level (fire once per statement).

Common use cases are auditing (an AFTER trigger copies every change into a history table with who and when), enforcing complex business rules that declarative constraints cannot express, maintaining derived or denormalized data (keeping a running balance or a summary count in sync), cascading custom logic, and making views updatable via INSTEAD OF. The advantages are automatic enforcement (the rule cannot be bypassed by forgetting to call it), centralization of the rule in one place regardless of which application touches the table, and guaranteed consistency because the trigger runs in the same transaction as the triggering statement.

The disadvantages are significant and worth stating as a senior. Triggers are "hidden" side effects — a simple `INSERT` can silently fire cascading logic that surprises developers and complicates debugging, because the behavior is invisible in the application code. They add overhead to every DML operation and can hurt performance on high-throughput tables. They are hard to version-control, test, and reason about, and poorly designed triggers can cause recursion or cascading trigger chains and even deadlocks. They also fragment business logic between the database and the application. The balanced guidance is to use triggers for cross-cutting, must-not-be-bypassed concerns tightly coupled to data — especially auditing and integrity that constraints cannot express — and to avoid pushing ordinary business logic into them, keeping triggers small, deterministic, and well-documented.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India must guarantee two things on its accounts table no matter which application writes to it: a deposit or balance change can never make a balance negative (a BEFORE rule that rejects the operation), and every balance change must be recorded in an immutable audit trail with the old and new values (an AFTER rule). Relying on each application to remember these was unsafe, so they moved the rules into triggers bound to the table.

Our mini-project simulates a trigger engine on an `accounts` table: a BEFORE-UPDATE trigger that validates the new balance and rejects negatives, and an AFTER-UPDATE trigger that appends an audit row with OLD and NEW balances — demonstrating the two timings, OLD/NEW row images, and how the rules fire automatically regardless of caller.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one account, A100, seeded with a balance of five thousand.

Step 1 — A valid update to seven thousand arrives. The BEFORE-UPDATE trigger runs first, checks that the new balance is not negative, and allows it to proceed.

Step 2 — The row is written, changing A100 to seven thousand. Immediately the AFTER-UPDATE trigger fires and appends an audit line recording the old value five thousand and the new value seven thousand — the application did nothing to request this; it happened automatically.

Step 3 — An invalid update to minus two hundred arrives. The BEFORE-UPDATE trigger runs, detects the negative balance, and rejects the operation by raising an error, which in a real engine rolls back the statement.

Step 4 — Because the BEFORE trigger rejected the change, the row is never written and the AFTER trigger never fires, so no audit line is added and the balance stays at seven thousand.

Step 5 — The final audit trail shows exactly one entry, for the valid change only, proving the triggers enforced validation and auditing automatically and consistently regardless of the caller.

Final output:

```text
A100 balance after valid update = 7000.0
Rejected: BEFORE UPDATE: balance for A100 cannot go negative (-200.0)
A100 balance unchanged after reject = 7000.0
Audit trail (written automatically by AFTER trigger):
  AUDIT A100: 5000.00 -> 7000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  UPDATE accounts SET balance=NEW WHERE account=?    (any application)
        │
        ▼
  ┌─ BEFORE UPDATE trigger ──────────────────────────────┐
  │ validate NEW; may modify NEW or RAISE (reject)        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │ passes                         │ fails → RAISE → rollback (no write, no AFTER)
        ▼
   [ row written: OLD → NEW ]
        │
        ▼
  ┌─ AFTER UPDATE trigger ───────────────────────────────┐
  │ react: append audit(OLD, NEW); cannot change the row  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  INSTEAD OF (on a VIEW): redirect insert/update to base tables
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Triggers as Non-Bypassable Rules ═══

  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐   all DML
  │ Web app   │  │ Batch job │  │ Admin tool│ ───────────┐
  └───────────┘  └───────────┘  └───────────┘            ▼
                                            ┌───────────────────────┐
                                            │ accounts table        │
                                            │ BEFORE: validate       │ ← cannot bypass
                                            │ AFTER : audit history   │
                                            └───────────────────────┘
  Advantages: automatic, centralized, same transaction (consistent)
  Disadvantages: hidden side effects, overhead, hard to test, recursion/deadlock risk
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Trigger Timings & OLD/NEW ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Observer/Hook: triggers react to DML events                       │
  │ Template: updateBalance = before → write → after                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: BEFORE validates; AFTER audits — separate concerns            │
  │ O: new rule = new trigger, callers unchanged                     │
  │ D: apps depend on table contract, triggers enforce invisibly     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Timings ──
  BEFORE     : before write | validate / modify NEW | can REJECT
  AFTER      : after write  | react / audit         | cannot change row
  INSTEAD OF : replace event| mainly on views        | redirect to base tables
  Granularity: row-level (OLD/NEW per row) vs statement-level

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main() → updateBalance(A100, 7000)
  2.   → beforeUpdate()  [OK]
  3.   → write row
  4.   → afterUpdate()   [append audit]
  5. updateBalance(A100, -200) → beforeUpdate() RAISES → no write, no audit
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A trigger is procedural code stored in the database that executes automatically in response to a data event such as `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on a table. Its timing determines what it can do. A BEFORE trigger runs before the row is written, so it can validate the incoming data and reject the operation by raising an error, or modify the new values, because it sees and can change the proposed row. An AFTER trigger runs once the change is already applied, so it cannot alter the row but can react to it — typically writing an audit record, updating a summary table, or sending a notification. An INSTEAD OF trigger replaces the triggering action entirely and is used mainly on views to make an otherwise non-updatable view updatable by translating the operation into changes on the base tables. Triggers can be row-level, firing once per affected row with access to the OLD and NEW row images, or statement-level.

The main use cases are auditing, enforcing complex business rules that declarative constraints cannot express, and keeping derived or denormalized data consistent, and the advantages are that the rule is enforced automatically and cannot be bypassed by forgetting to call it, it is centralized in one place for every application, and it runs in the same transaction as the triggering statement so consistency is guaranteed. At the National Bank of India we used a BEFORE-UPDATE trigger on the accounts table to reject any change that would make a balance negative and an AFTER-UPDATE trigger to append an immutable audit row with the old and new balances, so those rules held no matter which application wrote to the table. The disadvantages I always state honestly are that triggers are hidden side effects that make a simple `INSERT` silently fire cascading logic and complicate debugging, they add overhead to every DML operation, they are hard to version-control and test, and poorly designed ones can cause recursion, cascading trigger chains, or deadlocks. My balanced guidance is to use triggers for cross-cutting, must-not-be-bypassed concerns tightly coupled to data, especially auditing and integrity that constraints cannot express, and to keep ordinary business logic in the application. The line I always state is that a trigger fires automatically on DML — BEFORE to validate or modify, AFTER to react or audit, and INSTEAD OF to redirect, usually on views.
